learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected Mostly leaves into the air at a wide angle and locked the prediction for an underwater beam tilted 60 degrees from straight up.
observations.exploration: Started at 45 degrees: exit 70.5 degrees, 86% escaping and 14% reflected. Stepped to 47 degrees: exit 77.1, 74% escaping; 48 degrees: exit 82.1, 57% escaping. At 48.6 degrees the exit direction lay along the surface and escaping fraction was zero. Jumped to 60 degrees: no exit ray, 100% reflected.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to all reflected back down, accurately recounted the 45, 48.6 and 60 degree states, and explained that refraction away from the normal reaches a limit at a surface-parallel direction. It disclosed still flat water and one color of light.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot at 60 degrees. A yellow incident beam and reflected beam stayed below a flat blue surface, with no ray in the air. A dashed normal, 60 degree arc and 100% back label supported the readouts.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884163 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The prompt challenges extrapolating a wider emerging ray indefinitely.

interaction.reason: Fine preset steps expose the approach to the boundary and the beyond-boundary state.
interaction.evidence: Escaping light declined from 86% through 74% and 57% to zero before the 60 degree test.

payoff.reason: The reveal uses observed boundary states to explain total reflection.
payoff.evidence: It names the surface-grazing direction and absence of an exit direction beyond it.

clarity.reason: The ray diagram and fractions make the changing outcomes explicit.
clarity.evidence: The final screenshot shows both beams below the surface and no transmitted ray.

transfer.reason: The general optical condition is explained without a distinct new application.
transfer.evidence: No other material, device or fresh case is explored.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: Tilting more eventually prevents light escaping rather than spreading it farther.
surprise.evidence: At 60 degrees the surface reflects everything back into water.

visualExplanation.reason: The normal, ray directions and energy fractions support the explanation.
visualExplanation.evidence: At the final state the incident and reflected rays share the underwater side.

playfulness.reason: Small tilt steps make the critical transition discoverable.
playfulness.evidence: The one-step button exposes 47, 48 and 48.6 degrees before the jump.

practicalValue.reason: It builds intuition for total internal reflection.
practicalValue.evidence: The reveal states the boundary condition under ideal water assumptions.

depth.reason: It includes partial reflection approaching the critical angle.
depth.evidence: The original 14% reflection grows before complete reflection.

complexity.reason: One angle control is easy, while refraction relative to a normal and a critical angle require new spatial reasoning.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Moderate: distinguish incident and exit angles and understand their limiting relation.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low: slider, step button and 60 degree shortcut.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: The emerging direction reaches 90 degrees before the incident angle does.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Refraction, partial reflection and total internal reflection are introduced.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Moderate: angle arcs, normal line, rays and percentage fractions.

whyCool: A transparent surface becomes a mirror purely because of the direction of the incoming light.
caveat: The lesson assumes a still flat surface and one light color, with fixed materials.
missingEvidence: No different medium or real optical application was tested.
